data.title: Burial mounds of the West Slavs – the barrow regions of Central Europe and Slovakia
data.excerpt: Earthen mounds, mostly oval, are the typical Slavic way of burying the dead, and their mystical atmosphere still draws people a thousand years later. This survey covers the 15 barrow regions of Central Europe and the seven groups in Slovakia, the cremation and inhumation rites, the composition of the mounds and the modest grave goods they hold – and shows why digging them up in the hope of treasure is a mistaken idea.

children.text: Earthen mounds, mostly oval in shape and called burial mounds or barrows, are the typical Slavic way of burying the dead. Even after a thousand years their unrepeatable, mystical atmosphere still draws people to them. The mistake made by some enthusiasts, however, is that they try to dig them up in the hope of obtaining treasure from the barrow, which – as is clear from this article too – is a mistaken idea. On the digging up and looting of barrows Michal Lutovský writes, for example:

“in the case of Slavic barrows this is an entirely pointless activity. Today’s gold-diggers dig up nothing but poor rural cemeteries for the sake of a few sherds and corroded, shapeless scraps of iron.”
Slavic burial customs

The rite of cremating the dead is regarded as the Indo-European heritage of the Slavs. The change of rite – the burial of unburnt bodies in the ground – begins to appear gradually from the 8th century onwards under the influence of the environment with which the Slavs came into contact. The change was already taking place before the acceptance of Christianity, which merely accelerated the process.

blocks.author: Silent Stream of Godless Elegy

children.text: In the Slavic period the death of a member of the kin was bound up with a host of customs and rituals. The typical elements of the funeral rite include above all the custom of not carrying the dead person out of the house through the door or through the gate in the fence, but through a window, an opening in the wall, a hole under the threshold or an opening in the fence of the farmstead. The purpose was to confuse the soul of the deceased so that it could not find its way back and harm the survivors as a vampire or some other human demon. As late as the 19th century Pavol Dobšinský recorded this custom in the tale of Krásna Ibronka (Beautiful Ibronka): “Mark me, my dear neighbours, when I die, do not carry my coffin over the threshold and through the door, nor let the coffin be struck three times against the threshold, but have a pit dug beneath the threshold and draw my coffin out of the house through that hole. And harness to the little cart the pony we still have in the stable, and bury me there, where that pony comes to a halt with me!” Laudations, songs of praise and ritual weeping, accompanied by tearing at the face with the hands, by howling or by the cutting of hair and even self-wounding, were a generally widespread part of the funeral ritual. Their purpose was evidently an offering of blood and hair to the soul of the deceased.

In many regions the ancient custom of hiring mourning women for the ritual lament over the dead has survived. Their wailing and the funeral songs, which were meant to satisfy the soul of the dead person and to drive away evil spirits, were an absolutely indispensable part of the funeral procession. Symbolic games accompanied by singing, and feasts, also belonged to the funeral rite. A peculiarity of the Slavic funeral rite were the burials of widows or concubines. This was a voluntary death of the beloved woman, although her decision was influenced by what those around her expected. Women mostly carried out the suicide by hanging; at other times they burnt themselves alive, as was the case among the Indians and as Arab eyewitnesses described it, or they were strangled and stabbed after being drugged and after intercourse with those present, which concerned chiefly female slaves. The Indo-European notion was that life in the hereafter was a kind of continuation, albeit in another form, of earthly life with its physical needs, including food, drink and bodily love. That is why the deceased were equipped with the appropriate grave offerings and were not to live without their favourite women in the next world either. This custom, however, concerned above all members of the ruling class, since archaeological excavation does not detect it in the cemeteries of the common people. We have records, for example, of funerals that were held in woods and fields, and of games which, according to the pagan rite, were held at crossroads and road junctions. Part of the funeral performance was sometimes also a kind of mock combat of men, accompanied by shouting and the clashing of weapons, which can have had no other purpose than to drive away the evil demons threatening the soul of the deceased and the survivors. The funeral feast was called “strava”. It was preceded by an offering of food and drink to the dead person at the grave. Especially characteristic was the offering of an intoxicating drink, above all mead, which all the survivors indulged in after the funeral.

children.text: Cremation of the dead

After the deceased had been carried out and laid at the place where the cremation was to take place, the probable procedure was as follows. Once the funeral procession had arrived, the survivors laid the bier with the dead person, wrapped in hide or cloth, on the funeral pyre and placed the grave offerings beside them. These could be objects of which the dead person had been fond, but also various drinks and foods. The funeral pyre had a grillage construction and was about 1.8 m high, 2 m long and 1.2 m wide (Galuška). Building it consumed 3–4 m³ of wood. It was lit with fire brought either from the house of the deceased or with so-called living fire, produced by rubbing wood against wood directly at the site of the pyre. Experiments have shown that the complete burning of a body required about 10 hours of burning. It is clear that the further funerary steps could then follow only on the next day. The survivors then gathered up the parts of what remained of the funeral pyre, above all the charred pieces of bone, and carried them to the cemetery. There the remains were reverently placed either in a pottery vessel, which was buried in the ground, or, in a later period, in a barrow. The building of the barrows mostly followed only after the reverent deposition of the remains. Sometimes various timber structures – a kind of house of the dead – were even built to hold the remains. There are, however, also cases in which the barrow was built first and the remains were inserted into it.

children.text: Barrow regions of the West Slavs in Central Europe and Slovakia

In the former territory of the West Slavs in the early Middle Ages two ways of burying the dead are archaeologically recognisable: beneath barrow mounds and in grave pits in so-called flat cemeteries. Regions with a predominant barrow rite have been delimited territorially; their boundaries, however, can only be assumed approximately, because many barrows in agricultural and sub-montane terrain fell victim to the cultivation of the land. Given the destruction of sometimes whole cemeteries, their existence is often attested only by a place name (for example Homole, Na Mohylky) and their chronological assignment is unverifiable. At the barrow cemetery at Skalica, I. L. Červinka recorded about 100 barrows in 1922, while in 1943 V. Budinský-Krička measured only 63 of them. The geographical distribution of the barrow cemeteries in closed regions can be explained by the penetration of the Slavs into the territory of present-day Slovakia in several waves from different directions, and hence also with differing burial customs. (Lutovský 1989, 1996a; Váňa 1952).

children.text: In Central Europe
15 closed barrow regions have been delimited:

1. The South Bohemian–Austrian region is the most numerous, with burial in the 7th to 9th centuries. A common feature is the use of stone structures and the scattering of small burnt bones at the original ground level beneath the barrow mound.
2. The East Bohemian region – with a characteristic so-called lower mound and burial in the 7th–9th centuries.
3. The Moravian–West Slovak region, with a predominance of biritual and inhumation barrow cemeteries, where burial begins in the 8th century and ends during the first half of the 10th century.
4. The Upper Nitra region – with an early transition from the cremation barrow rite to inhumation barrow burial. Barrows were built here from the 7th to the 9th century.
5. The Váh region is ritually inconsistent, with a slow demise of cremation burial and a larger number of biritual barrow cemeteries. Chronological assignment: the 8th–9th century.

blocks.alt: Barrow regions of the West Slavs in Central Europe and Slovakia

children.text: 6. The Turiec region – a common feature is the small extent of the barrow cemeteries and the deposition of inhumation burials at the original level of the surrounding terrain. These are graves from the beginning of the 9th century.

7. The East Slovak–Subcarpathian region (including Transcarpathian Ukraine) – typical is the scattering of small burnt bones at the original ground level and the long survival of the cremation barrow rite. Dating: the 8th–9th century, only at Topoľovka as late as the 11th century.

8. The Lusatian region – a common feature is the use of stones in the mounds of the barrows, so-called paving, and also timber structures; the barrows were built from the middle of the 7th century to the turn of the 10th and 11th centuries.

9. The Silesian region – has greater variability in the construction of the barrows; in the Upper Oder group a lower mound is frequent, the Wrocław group used stone structures, and common to them was the use of rectangular timber structures. Barrow burial survived from the 7th to the 9th century.

10. The North Carpathian region, from the San to the Vistula and in the south as far as the Carpathians – only the Kraków group has distinctive features, a lower mound in combination with stone and timber elements. The barrow rite began in the 7th century and ended in the 11th century.

11. The Lublin–Sandomierz region: typical is the small extent of the cemeteries, with burial beginning as early as the 6th century and ending in the 11th century. It was evidently from the westernmost region of Sandomierz that the barrow rite spread eastwards.

12. The Bug–Białystok region is distinguished by barrows with larger mounds and by burial from the 6th century onwards. The greatest development of the rite took place in the 10th to 12th centuries. These facts have made it possible to link the barrows already with the East Slavs.
13. The Lower Havel region is known for the use of earthen mounds surrounded by circular ditches. Barrow burial begins in the 7th and ends in the 9th century.
14. The region of the left bank of the Elbe: remains of extensive cremation sites (funeral pyres) were found beneath the mounds; the barrows are of the 8th–9th century.

15. The region of the Baltic coast: it comprises the northern part of Poland and Germany, with barrows strongly represented in the area of the Bay of Lübeck and on Rügen. Of interest is the concentration of barrow cemeteries near the coast, for example around Wolin. (The second, Volhynian region on the Polish–Ukrainian borderland is already linked with the East Slavic barrow rite; East Slavic cultural elements predominate among the finds. The Volyň hillfort in the Bug region was smaller than Aksmanica, with an area of 2.8 ha, and may have been only one of the less important centres of the Volhynians. Some Polish historians linked the mention of them in the Bavarian Geographer with the Wolinians by the Baltic, while Ukrainian and Russian historians linked it with the Volhynians in the Bug region. Ondrej R. Halaga, 1985)
The barrow rite in the region began in the 8th century and ended along the whole coast in the 12th century. (M. Lutovský 1989)
In the territory of Slovakia
the barrow rite predominates in seven regions (M. Hanuliak 2001):

blocks.alt: Barrow regions of the West Slavs in Central Europe and Slovakia

children.text: 1. The Záhorie group: Gbely, Skalica – about 115 barrows.
2. The Middle Váh group: about 23 barrows, Borovce, Trenčín.
3. The North Váh group: Beluša, Dolný Moštenec, Orlové, Sverepec, Prečín, Bohunice, Visolaje, about 135 barrows in all.
4. The Žilina–Čadča group: with 162 barrows, Bitarová, Divina, Dolný Vadičov, Hôrky, Kotrčiná Lúčka, Krasňany, Krásno nad Kysucou, Žilina (Bánová, Teplička nad Váhom, Závodie).
5. The Upper Nitra group: 58 barrows in all at the sites of Brezolupy, Diviaky nad Nitricou, Ješkova Ves, Mačov, Koš, Nemčeky, Veľké Hoste, Vysočany.
6. The Turiec group: 13 barrows in all, recorded at Blatnica, Malý Čepčín, Martin in the Priekopa district, Moškovec, Sučany, Turany, Turčianske Jaseno, Veľký Čepčín and Žabokreky.
7. The Zemplín–Ondava group: Malý Horeš, Kráľovský Chlmec, Streda nad Bodrogom, Topoľovka, and 108 barrows in all (M. Hanuliak 2001).

This list of sites is only approximate. Given the typically low number of objects placed in Slavic barrows, or their complete absence, their destruction in the cremation rite, or the lack of anthropological material, it was sometimes impossible even after excavation to determine the period and to assign them to the Slavs. In the period of the earlier archaeological excavations cremation barrows were even considered empty, since the few scattered small burnt bones in the mounds of the barrows easily escaped attention.

blocks.alt: Barrow regions of the West Slavs in Central Europe and Slovakia

children.text: The barrow rite and ritual

The ground plan of Slavic barrows is circular, oval or occasionally elongated with rounded corners. The present-day size ranges from a diameter of 4 m in the case of circular barrows (for example Orlové) to a length of 27 m in the case of the oval barrow at Skalica. The original height of the mounds is unknown; the barrows are exposed to weathering, or have slumped into the ditch around their perimeter, and have therefore undergone various post-depositional transformations.

The barrow rite appears in the 6th century and ends roughly in the 10th century, on the Baltic coast in the 12th century; in the north of Russia barrows are not unusual even in the 16th century. In the case of individual barrow cemeteries, a long or a short chronology is considered. If a barrow cemetery had been used by a larger community, it would have been exhausted in a short time. The long chronology is more probable, as is proved by dated finds from biritual barrow cemeteries. The barrow rite begins as a cremation rite; around the middle of the 9th century it changes to inhumation, that is, the burial of unburnt bodies. At some barrow cemeteries both cremation and inhumation burials were found – so-called biritual barrow cemeteries. In the case of a long chronology, that is, a long period of burial at a barrow cemetery, there are too few barrows at these cemeteries, and the question arises where the rest of the dead from the regions of exclusively barrow burial are (Lutovský 1989, 1990). The number of barrows in Slovakia is approximately 614; for comparison, the number of flat graves of the 9th–10th centuries is about 3,239 (Hanuliak 2001). Not all the dead from such extensive barrow regions can have been buried at the barrow cemeteries, even when the number of destroyed barrow cemeteries and the fact that one barrow may contain several burials are taken into account. We do not know the number of dead in cremation barrows; in inhumation barrows there is often one dead person, at Skalica for example 2 to 5 individuals, and the largest barrow, no. 13, contained as many as 11 graves (Kraskovská 1992). Barrows represent raised ground, and probably for that reason secondary graves too are sunk into the mounds; in the village of Přítluky further dead were buried by inhumation in older Slavic barrows in the 11th century (Poulík 1951). Empty barrows – cenotaphs – are so far attested in the whole Slavic territory only on Rügen and at Gnezdovo in Russia.

There are traditionally few artefacts in Slavic barrows; what matters is their spatial distribution within the mound and the composition of the mound itself, which indicate how the funeral rituals proceeded. In the documentation of the first excavations, if any was made at all, it is precisely this information that is missing. Excavation was limited to a central cut into the barrow. Hearths, stone and timber structures and lower mounds have been identified in the mounds of Slavic barrows. During the excavation of the mound at Bezemín it was found that they did not wait for the timber structure to burn out; the barrow was heaped up over a still burning “pyre”, as is proved by the burnt stones beside the remains of the wood (Kudrnáč 1951).

blocks.alt: Barrow regions of the West Slavs in Central Europe and Slovakia

children.text: The cremation rite

Burnt bones were not deposited according to a single rite; the system was not fixed, and differences existed not only between the barrow regions but also within a single cemetery. Small calcined bones have been found scattered over the original level of the surrounding ground, dispersed singly or in groups throughout the whole body of the barrow, deposited in a small pit, poured out on the surface of the lower mound, in an urn in the mantle and also at the base of the barrow; urns were also placed on the surface of the barrow, and even on posts projecting from the barrows. This above-barrow burial among the East Slavs was described by Nestor: the bones were placed in a small vessel and it was set up on posts beside the roads. Above-barrow burial was recorded at Vitějovice and at Kožlí near Orlík; in such a case fragments of pottery are found on the slope and at the base of the barrow (Lutovský 1996a, 1996b, 2012). At Bulhary no traces of burial at all were found directly in the barrow mound; fragments of two vessels lay in the ditch beside the barrow. It is assumed that they were originally deposited together with the burial on the top of the barrow, from where they slid down its slope over time into the ditch that surrounded it (Nekvasil 1955). Another way of depositing the urn was recorded at Veľké Hoste, where a vessel with incompletely burnt bones was sunk into the mantle of the barrow at a depth of about 30 cm (Točík 1978).

In regions with a predominant lower mound, the ash together with a small quantity of small burnt bones is found scattered on the surface of this compact body, which was subsequently covered with the mantle of the barrow. This method is widespread in north-eastern Bohemia, in the Prachov Rocks, at Nadslav, Vinařice and Dvakačovice (Turčan 1984). Small groups of burnt bones dispersed throughout the whole body of the barrow were found at Bezemín (Kudrnáč 1951). At Vysočany on the Dyje, cremation burials were poured out at the original level of the surrounding ground beneath the barrow mound (Král 1955).

blocks.alt: Barrow regions of the West Slavs in Central Europe and Slovakia

children.text: A further method is the deposition of incompletely burnt fragments of bone in a small pit. At Kráľovský Chlmec all the barrows examined were cremation barrows with two or more burials in a single barrow; the small pits had been dug into the lower body or the subsoil of the barrow. A few burnt bones were also found in smaller groups in the mounds of the barrows (Budinský-Krička 1950). In eastern Slovakia the cremation rite predominates and almost all the methods of depositing burials mentioned are attested – in a dug pit, in small heaps, in the torso of a vessel – in the earlier period. A probably later phase was the scattering of small crushed, incompletely burnt bones at ground level or throughout the whole mound. In central Slovakia dispersal at the original ground level predominates (Hanuliak 2001). At biritual Skalica a great variability of the cremation rite was recorded, from deposition in cremation urns, in dug pits, in small heaps and at the original ground level, to one case in which the remains were left on the cremation site (Kraskovská 1992). The second largest barrow cemetery in north-western Slovakia is Visolaje. In 1960 the Považie Museum recorded the cremation rite there, with small pits sunk into the subsoil. In barrow no. 2 the earth in the fill of the pit was most intensively burnt through and contained the greatest quantity of bone. A fire had evidently burned in the pit.

blocks.alt: Barrow regions of the West Slavs in Central Europe and Slovakia

children.text: Of interest is the find of cremation graves between the barrows at the site of Přítluky as well (Poulík 1951), and a kind of system for improving the draught during burning at Veselí nad Lužnicí. Rectangular trench-like pits and shallow, obliquely running pits had been dug into the weathered rock beneath the barrow mounds. In the second barrow, stones had been set into the wall of such a pit as if to allow a draught. No burial was found in any of the pits, which supported this idea (Turek 1952). A phenomenon so far isolated in Slovakia is the stone setting around incompletely burnt bones. At Kráľovský Chlmec a round barrow contained 3 cremation burials; in the southern part of the barrow there was a stone chamber made of three stones, beneath it charcoal and ash, and towards the west there was a cremation site 1 m in diameter with burnt earth. The dead had been cremated in the southern part of the barrow (Pastor 1951).

From this list it is clear that beneath a single cremation barrow, besides charred timber structures, ash and incompletely burnt bones, smaller burnt patches – hearths – were also found, on which cremation could not have taken place because of their small size. The lighting of these fires is an expression of ritual ceremonies (Lutovský 1996a).

blocks.alt: Barrow regions of the West Slavs in Central Europe and Slovakia

children.text: There is little evidence for the cremation of the dead directly at the place where the barrow was to be heaped up. In Slovakia it is barrow no. 14 at Kráľovský Chlmec (Budinský-Krička 1980), in Bohemia Kožlí near Orlík. Cremation sites, that is, the places at which the Slavs burnt their dead, have so far not been found. On the basis of ethnographic surveys, cremation could have taken place directly in the settlements (Turčan 1984). The pyre, however, need not necessarily have stood at the settlement or at the cemetery. During the excavations of the cemeteries the area between the barrows was partly uncovered as well. So far evidence of a large fire is everywhere lacking, and there should be about 3,000 cm³ of burnt bone, not a few scattered fragments (Lutovský 1996a).
The inhumation rite

The inhumation rite begins at the turn of the 8th and 9th centuries; it replaced the older cremation burial. The new way of burying may have been brought by groups migrating under pressure from the Avar Khaganate (Hanuliak 2001). In the inhumation rite too, various ways of laying out the dead appeared, either at ground level beneath the barrow mound, or in grave pits, rectangular or with niches, dug into the subsoil of the barrows. For lack of data obtained from the barrow cemeteries examined so far, it cannot be proved in Slovakia that burial at ground level preceded burial in grave pits. Skeletons from ground level are often completely decayed, which has made anthropological examination and a detailed chronology impossible. The discovery of grave pits beneath the barrows at Bánová also put an end to speculation about burial at the original ground level in mountainous and rocky territories where pits are difficult to dig. At Stěbořice the grave pits had likewise been dug down into the weathered rock; a male skeleton lay in a wooden frame and a female one in a coffin (Jisl 1953). In the grave pits of the Slavs various timber arrangements frequently occur, both in barrows and in flat cemeteries. Remains of timber arrangements have also been found in burials at ground level. At Sverepec, in barrow no. 3, the skeleton was oriented E–W. By the skull bone there was an 85 cm long undulating band of charcoal running N–S, which may have arisen from the dry distillation of wood; the dead person had been set about with wood in the manner of a coffin. The 85 cm long band of charcoal indicates the width of the coffin or of the timber setting. To the south of the skeleton, beneath the barrow mound, a bed of embers was found. This was present in inhumation barrow no. 4 as well, and in barrow no. 2 there were two beds of embers (Petrovský-Šichman 1968). Both ways of laying out inhumation burials were recorded, for example, at Skalica and at Veľké Hoste. At Skalica one man was buried in a coffin hollowed out of an oak trunk; in some cases the body lay in a coffin of oak boards (Kraskovská 1959). At the biritual barrow cemetery at Veľké Hoste there were grave pits in 6 cases, and in 9 barrows the dead lay at ground level. The sunken pits had larger dimensions, up to 330 × 200 cm, and in two pits traces of a ritual fire were found. Barrow no. 6, round, 9 m in diameter and 0.35 m high, with a grave pit 1.25 m deep, bore traces of a larger fire. Pieces of burnt wood were found on the bottom of the pit and in its corners. It is an inhumation grave combined with the cremation rite: a timber pyre had been built in the grave pit and the dead person was partly burnt. Above this burial there was yet another dead person in the same pit (Porubský 1954). Two grave pits beneath one barrow were found at Bánová; they contained the unburnt bodies of warriors covered with tree bark. There were weapons in the barrow, and the grave pits, exceptional for north-western Slovakia, likewise testify to the presence of members of Great Moravian military retinues of the 9th century (Moravčík 1975). Shallower or deeper grave pits were present at Skalica as well, with various timber arrangements; the walls were lined on two or four sides with boards and beams. Some of the dead lay on a wooden support or were covered with a board from above. Just as at Bánová, here too dead people were found laid on tree bark, or moss had been spread on the bottom of the pit (Kraskovská 1992). Of interest is the note from Stěbořice, where the fill of the grave pit was so loose that once it had been uncovered, arched traces of the cutting out of the pit were visible on its walls – probably made with an axe. In the wall behind the head of the skeleton there was a niche. The depth of the pits was up to 155 cm (Jisl 1953).

blocks.alt: Barrow regions of the West Slavs in Central Europe and Slovakia

children.text: According to Slavic custom the dead were laid out E–W, with the feet to the east and the head to the west, so that their face was turned towards the sunrise. At the barrow cemeteries slight deviations in the directions NE–SW and the like also occur as a rule. At Skalica, for example, 61 of the dead had the basic E–W orientation and 5 had a N–S and NE–SW orientation (Kraskovská 1992). The largest Slavic barrow cemetery in north-western Slovakia, biritual Krasňany with 51 barrows, had inhumation graves laid at the original ground level and oriented E–W (Moravčík 1975). A different orientation, N–S, was recorded in barrow no. 2 at Beluša – Koscelišče and in two barrows at Sverepec – Podvrščie. The almost completely decayed skeletons had been set about with stones in the shape of a rectangle running N–S. A list of graves with exceptional orientation at the Moravian cemeteries was drawn up by B. Dostál. V. Hrubý, for his part, stated that members of a different ethnic origin may be sought in these graves, and for that reason A. Petrovský-Šichman raised the question, in connection with Sverepec, whether these were not warriors of foreign origin who nevertheless used the Slavic objects present in the barrows. The stone setting around the remains of the skeleton in barrow no. 1 was also so narrow (25 cm) that the dead person must have been laid on their side and not on their back, as was usual among the Slavs (Petrovský-Šichman 1968). One of the possible causes of the slight deviations from the east–west direction towards the north or the south could be the position of the sun in different seasons of the year, or difficulties in determining sunrise exactly in the early Middle Ages at cemeteries with a poor view of the horizon.

blocks.alt: Barrow regions of the West Slavs in Central Europe and Slovakia

children.text: Biritual barrows and barrow cemeteries

The joint occurrence of the cremation and the inhumation rite at one barrow cemetery is a transitional phase from the cremation of the dead in the 7th–8th centuries to the burial of unburnt bodies, which took shape in the first half of the 9th century. The process of the transformation of the rites can best be observed at the cemeteries that have been examined almost in their entirety, such as biritual Krasňany, Skalica and Veľké Hoste, where cremation and inhumation barrows occur together. Birituality is abundantly represented in the Upper Nitra group of barrows. In the present state of research it appears that the barrow cemeteries in the valley of the Bebrava, such as Veľké Hoste, Brezolupy and Jerichov, have several similar features. The cremation barrows are larger in size than the inhumation ones, there is only one grave in each barrow, and the most frequent grave offerings are objects belonging to the equipment of a warrior (Porubský 1954).

blocks.alt: Barrow regions of the West Slavs in Central Europe and Slovakia

children.text: An expression of the untroubled replacement of the rites may be the existence of barrows which contain both a cremation and an inhumation grave beneath one mound (Hanuliak 2001). At Bitarová, in barrow no. 17 with a diameter of 10 m, there was a cremation grave in the mound of the barrow and beneath the mound two inhumation graves oriented SW–SE and E–W; one of the dead was in the eastern part of the barrow, the other in the western part (Budinský-Krička 1957). A biritual barrow was also present at Beluša – Koscelišče, where in 1963 both cremation and inhumation burial was recorded beneath one mound at the original ground level. The inhumation grave was buried under stones (Petrovský-Šichman 1964). Likewise at Skalica, cremation and inhumation graves were found beneath one barrow; at Krasňany near Žilina an oval barrow contained two inhumation and two cremation graves.

In as many as 31% of the barrow cemeteries examined in the territory of Slovakia, not one of the three rites mentioned can be confirmed unambiguously. Eight cemeteries are given as biritual, although only one or two barrows have been examined (Hanuliak 2001).
Long barrows, collective and cumulative barrows.

The oval long barrows of the West Slavs can be found throughout Central Europe – in Bohemia, Moravia, Poland and Slovakia, and to a lesser extent in Germany. We regard as collective only those long barrows which consist of several barrow mounds (regardless of the number of burials), which is common in the East Slavic milieu. Their long barrows were created by the gradual addition of individual mounds; the final length reaches as much as 40 m and they contain up to 22 cremation burials (Lutovský 1996a). An example of a collective barrow from the territory of Bohemia is the double barrow at Bechyňská Smoleč, and from Slovakia Borovce near Piešťany.

The size of the long barrows of the West Slavs is around 20 m; at Skalica, barrow no. 22 measured as much as 27 m. The first Czech excavations of such barrows were carried out by Rudolf Turek at Veselí nad Lužnicí; the long barrows had mounds of differing composition. For example, the oval barrow no. 3, running west–east, originally had its core on the eastern side, where there was a lower body of yellow clay; on its surface there was an ashy layer, and further layers of clay and gravel rested on it, while in the upper part a band of scattered small burnt bones ran along its whole length. The barrow had several burials, evidently a double cremation burial on the western side and a further cremation burial above the eastern base of the barrow (Turek 1952). A long cremation barrow was also examined at Dvakačovice. Barrow no. 6, measuring 16.4 × 10.8 m and 130 cm high, had a simple structure with a lower rammed body, on which an upper layer of clay was laid, mixed with charcoal and smaller remains of burnt wood. On the western, eastern and northern sides it was surrounded by ditches (Turčan 1984).

The construction of the so-called cumulative barrow at Kožlí near Orlík is unique: the barrow was formed from four mounds arranged in a square, and burials were present beneath only two of them. A wooden post was sunk into the ground and secured with stones, and a small mound was heaped up around it. A fire was lit at its base. While the fire was still burning, the barrow was heaped up further. In the immediate vicinity another barrow was built by the same procedure. Vessels with ash were placed on the posts. The further procedure was exceptional. On the western side of these barrows a space was bounded with stones, a mighty fire was lit and, while it was still burning, it was covered over with stones and earth; two vessels were smashed on top. All the mounds were covered with stones and a fourth barrow of earth was heaped up. Burials were present only in the first two barrows – on the posts; everything else formed part of funerary ceremonies that are not known in detail (Lutovský 1996b).

blocks.alt: A long barrow

children.text: At the biritual barrow cemetery at Brezolupy there were four barrows, two round and two oval. The oval barrow no. 1 was 12 m long and 65 cm high. At a depth of 20–25 cm below the level of the surrounding ground, 2 inhumation graves lay along the long axis of the barrow, oriented with the head to the west. Near each grave there was one burnt patch. Barrow no. 4, also oval, oriented N–S, 16 m long, 12 m wide and 105 cm high, was biritual. Scattered fragments of burnt bone were found in the middle of the mound. Further burials lay close to ground level; one was an inhumation, without a coffin, the skeleton oriented with the head to the west, the other was an urned burial with a burnt patch 185 cm long and 130 cm wide containing fragments of burnt wood, and the cremation urn, handmade, was almost completely preserved, with burnt bones in it. To the north-west there was another cremation grave with a burnt patch of 290 × 150 cm containing fragments of burnt wood and burnt bones. The last grave in this barrow was an urned burial with fragments of incompletely burnt bones (Budaváry 1935). At the biritual barrow cemetery at Jerichov the oval barrow no. 4, running north–south, measured 16.20 × 9.35 m and was 130 cm high. It was a cremation barrow and contained incompletely burnt small bones scattered in the barrow mound together with fragments of vessels and of burnt wood. The fires had been lit before the building of the mound began. At a depth of 105 cm from the top of the barrow, in the south-western part, a burnt patch of 120 × 70 cm was uncovered, whose ashy layer was 4 cm thick. To the west there was a small hearth. In the south-eastern part, at the level of the surrounding ground, there was another hearth 50 cm in diameter with a burnt layer 8–10 cm thick. The dead from the cremation graves at Jerichov had been burnt outside the barrows (Budaváry 1935).
The barrow mounds.

blocks.caption: Two barrows from the Váh region
blocks.alt: Two barrows from the Váh region

children.text: The composition of the barrow mound is the most essential thing; it has greater evidential value than the artefacts placed in the barrows themselves, for it betrays the traces of rituals. The mound may be homogeneous, with a lower body, or with rectangular stone or timber structures. The lower body, that is, the mound, is the primary barrow, onto which further layers were heaped. It differs from the deposit above it in hardness and compactness. This ramming of the lower mound is characteristic, for example, of the East Bohemian and South Bohemian regions – Bojetice, Dvakačovice, Nadslav, the Prachov Rocks, Vinařice. In the cremation rite the cremated remains were often scattered over the surface of such a lower mound. At Dvakačovice the layers of the lower body differed in colour and composition in section only in barrows 1, 6 and 9, whereas barrows 3 and 4 had both layers heaped up from the same material and differed only in their compactness. In barrow no. 4 these layers were additionally separated by a thin clayey layer. According to the initial assumptions, the lower body came into being through being trampled down during ritual dances, which could have developed into the sporting combats attested among the Russian Slavs (Turčan 1984). Lower mounds were documented at Veselí nad Lužnicí as well. Barrow no. 1 had, beneath its upper light sandy-loam mound, a more darkly coloured lower mound, and their interface was covered with irregularly laid stones. Barrow no. 4, for its part, had been heaped up from sand of two shades, so that it was possible to distinguish the lower body (Turek 1952). Documenting the composition of the barrow mound was often impossible at the Slovak barrow cemeteries, since rescue excavation followed only after their destruction during forestry and agricultural work. Examples are Sverepec – Podvrščie and Kráľovský Chlmec, where in 1966 the site was already a protected archaeological monument, yet 21 barrows were destroyed during the removal of the forest cover. The remaining cremation barrows at Kráľovský Chlmec, uncovered during systematic excavations, had been built of earth from the immediate vicinity, without the use of stone; the only exception was barrow no. 3, which contained a band of stones in the surface layer of the mound (Budinský-Krička 1980).
Timber structures.

blocks.alt: Barrow regions of the West Slavs in Central Europe and Slovakia

children.text: “Houses of the dead”, that is, internal rectangular timber structures in the barrows, were used in most of the Central European barrow regions of the West Slavs – in Slovakia, Moravia, Bohemia, Lesser Poland, Silesia and Lusatia. Frames of charred wood were documented in Bohemia for the first time in 1922 by Josef Antonín Jíra at Hlohovičky, but they were published only seventy years later. They were recorded completely only in the Prachov Rocks and at Nadslav, and after a further twenty years in Lesser Poland in the excavations of Helena Zoll-Adamikowa (Lutovský 2012). The side of a frame is usually 3–4 m long; the differences lie in the method of construction, which may use roundwood, boards or tree branches. Differences in construction can be observed even within a single cemetery, for example at Kožlí near Orlík. Part of the rite of transition from the world of the living was the destruction of the structure by fire. This procedure was applied at Vitějovice as well: the frame found in the barrow measured 3 × 3 m with its corners oriented to the cardinal points. The whole structure had passed through fire; the earth around it was burnt red, in places to a depth of 20 cm (Lutovský 2012). At the biritual barrow cemetery at Kožlí, rectangular timber structures were built in both cremation and inhumation barrows; oak was used, and to a lesser extent pine and fir. The hearths found in the cumulative barrows also contained oak wood (Lutovský 1996b). In the large elongated barrow at Dvakačovice, remains of burnt wood were found together with charcoal (Turčan 1984). Burnt timber structures are attested from the barrows of Bezemín as well. They lit the “pyre” and, while it was still burning, threw earth over it; they did not wait for it to burn out (Kudrnáč 1951). In the Váh barrow group, charred remains of rectangular timber structures were found in the cremation barrows of biritual Bitarová, measuring 4 × 4 m, with layers of burnt earth around them. After the structure had been set alight, the mound was heaped up over it, so that in the end it only smouldered. At Bánová, earth burnt in the shape of a square was recorded in the barrows, the trace of a timber frame (Moravčík 1975). At the biritual barrow cemetery at Krasňany, barrow no. 24 contained an inhumation grave oriented NW–SE at the level of the original surrounding ground, surrounded by narrow bands of dark earth in the shape of a rectangle. The grave had originally been lined on all four sides with wooden poles, the longer ones on the eastern side projecting beyond the shorter ones. In barrow no. 29 the dead person was set about with wood on only two sides, and likewise in barrow no. 38 (Budaváry 1938–1939). The timber structures of the West Slavs were not built for the stability of the mounds; they were set alight before the barrow was built, but the wood did not manage to burn out, as is proved by its transformation into charcoal (which is produced by burning without access to air). The structures are an expression of funerary rituals not known to us in detail. In cases where the wood burnt out completely, burnt earth remained visible in the place (Lutovský 1996a).
Stone structures and stone elements in the barrows.

blocks.alt: Barrow regions of the West Slavs in Central Europe and Slovakia

children.text: Stone structures serving to strengthen the barrows of the Slavs are less widespread in the territory of Slovakia, Bohemia and Moravia. In regions with a stony geological subsoil, irregularly distributed stones form part of the mounds, into which they found their way from the place where the material for building the barrow was taken. Exceptionally the stones form a cluster in the middle of the barrow, the so-called core, a stone circle along the outer perimeter of the barrow – a kerb, or a covering on the surface of the barrow called the mantle. Stone was used to a marked degree at Bezemín, where some barrows were for the most part built of stones laid flat. Barrow B was built of three layers of stones laid closely side by side; three of the stones were of the large size of 125 × 60 × 25 cm (Kudrnáč 1951). A stone core of the barrow was recorded in the barrows at Kožlí near Orlík. In cumulative barrow no. 2 the stones formed a mantle in the western part of the barrow and, beneath it, a three-layer core as well. At Vitějovice stones bordered the rectangular timber structure on the outside (Lutovský 1996b, 2012). In the Slovak barrow regions stone structures were recorded only rarely. At Kráľovský Chlmec, barrow no. 5 contained 3 cremation burials, one of which lay beneath a stone chamber consisting of three stones. In barrow no. 6 a cremation grave was placed at the original ground level beneath a larger, long stone, around which small bones were dispersed. These had been set about on the southern, eastern and western sides with further stones forming the structure of the barrow (Pastor 1951). At the second barrow cemetery at Kráľovský Chlmec, barrow no. 3 had a band of stones 60 cm wide in the surface layer on the crown of the barrow (Budinský-Krička 1950). Stone elements were used at Sverepec – Podvrščie as well. Small stones were set into the band of charcoal in inhumation barrow no. 1 in the shape of a rectangle of 60 × 170 cm, with the longer axis running N–S. The stones marked out the position of the dead person. In barrow no. 2 two large stones were placed at the feet of the dead person (Petrovský-Šichman 1964). In barrow no. 6 at Kožlí a prominent flat stone was set upright. The dead in barrows 8 and 9 also had large stones at their feet. After the barrow had been heaped up, the stones remained whole beneath the mound; they did not project above the surface of the barrow and were not visible. In the space between the barrows, just below the surface, stone paving was found, on which the funeral ceremony may have taken place. Large and heavy blocks of stone cannot have found their way into the barrows by chance while material for the mound was being taken; they must have been placed there deliberately (Lutovský 1996a).
Ditches around the barrows.

blocks.alt: Barrow regions of the West Slavs in Central Europe and Slovakia

children.text: On the outer perimeter of some barrows there are hollows of varying depth and width, which came into being through the removal of soil for heaping up the barrow mounds; their further function is not certain. One possibility is an attempt to drain off groundwater so that the barrows did not stand in a damp environment. The barrow cemeteries would then have to lie in terrain that was wet and marshy at the time. A further and more probable alternative is that the ditches had a cult significance. According to Helena Zoll-Adamikowa, hollows filled with water, or at least wetter than their surroundings, could have separated the world of the dead from the world of the living. The barrow cemeteries in southern Bohemia, which have stronger links to hillforts than to unfortified settlements, are always separated from one another by precisely a watercourse. During A. Knor’s excavation at Dvakačovice it was found that the hollow around barrow no. 6 disappears on the southern side, and likewise on the south-western side of barrow no. 9. The fact that the ditches had not been dug around the whole perimeter of the barrow and disappeared on the southern side was also reported by H. Zoll-Adamikowa at several cemeteries in Poland and by V. Kucharenko in the area of Novo Miropolje on the river Sluč. This “little bridge” on the southern side may be connected with the cult of the sun (Turčan 1984). At Bulhary the hollows around the individual barrows were recognised only after the area between the barrows had been uncovered over its whole extent. Barrow no. 1 had ditches of unequal width on its south-western, south-eastern and north-eastern sides. Barrow no. 2, for its part, was surrounded by a semicircular ditch beginning in the south and ending in the north-east. Fragments of pottery were found in the ditches of the barrows; cremation burials may originally have been placed on the top of the barrow in a cremation urn, which disintegrated over time and slid down the slope into the ditch at the base of the barrow (Nekvasil 1955). The most extensive barrow, 12 m in diameter and 1.5 m high, at Lhota on the river Mže, is surrounded by a ditch 1.6–2.4 m wide; at Veselí nad Lužnicí, barrow no. 2 had a hollow on its northern and eastern perimeter, and clearly visible ditches were also reported by J. Jisl at Stěbořice. At Vitějovice, ditches 1 m wide surrounded the individual barrows built in the middle of the barrow cemetery. At Bitarová, in the Váh barrow region, barrow no. 17 had a ditch on its southern and northern sides; the surroundings of the barrow were reportedly permanently marshy, and so the owner of the land filled the ditches in (Budinský-Krička 1957). At Sverepec – Podvrščie, beside inhumation barrow no. 1, shallow ditches had been dug beneath the southern and western edge of the barrow, evidently the source of the material for the mound (Petrovský-Šichman 1968). At Veľké Hoste one of the large cremation barrows was examined; the earth for its mound had been taken from the ditch around its perimeter (Porubský 1954).
Posts in the barrows.

Posts are a further type of timber structure in the barrows; their existence is archaeologically attested by finds of post holes lined with stones. Cremation urns with a burial could be placed directly on the posts, as Nestor described this funerary custom among the East Slavs. A second alternative is the view of S. A. Azjumova that the posts in the barrows may have been topped with figures of Slavic deities. Traces of the use of posts have survived in the names of cemeteries as well. At Teplička near Žilina the barrow cemetery lies at the locality known as Kolianske, and in Moravia the name Kůlové pole, denoting a place of Slavic graves, has survived. The old Slavic custom of setting up posts in barrows is attested by post holes recorded, for example, at Bitarová, Bánová and Sverepec. At Podvrščie near Sverepec a post hole was found in the middle of the barrow, lined with stones on the walls and on the bottom. The diameter of the hole was 40 cm and its depth 30 cm below the original ground surface (Petrovský-Šichman 1964, 1968).

children.text: The barrow inventory

Obtaining artefacts from Slavic cemeteries, which are as a rule poor in finds, is not a priority; their spatial distribution is more important. The characteristic simplicity of the grave goods is not a reflection of the poverty of the Slavs; it is only apparent, deliberate, and is the result of funerary customs. The presence of members of the ruling elite may be indicated by the size of the barrow mound, the size of the grave pit and its arrangement, the central position of the barrow within the cemetery or, on the contrary, its isolation. The overwhelming percentage of the finds consists of fragments of pottery. Whole vessels were smashed outside the barrow in connection with some funerary ritual and thrown into the mound. It is not always possible to reconstruct a whole vessel – only part of the sherds found their way into the barrow, and it cannot be ruled out that the survivors brought sherds collected from around their dwelling, which is how pottery of earlier cultures found its way into the barrows. Some earlier fragments found their way into the barrows from the place where the material for the mound was taken. Chipped stone blade tools and polished whetstones could have found their way into them in the same way; they are often evidence of occupation of the site by earlier prehistoric cultures.

blocks.alt: Barrow regions of the West Slavs in Central Europe and Slovakia

children.text: Objects of everyday use were placed in the barrows: knives (in the graves of women as well as men), spindle whorls, sickles, strike-a-light stones and buckets. To a lesser extent jewellery: glass beads,
gombíky

(spherical hollow dress ornaments) and earrings. Finds of parts of their equipment are regarded as evidence of the presence of warriors and horsemen: axes, arrowheads, spearheads, javelin heads and, exceptionally, a sword. The iron tools and weapons are poorly preserved and deformed by rust. Some barrows from Sverepec, Krasňany and Bánová are described as warriors’ barrows. Exceptionally, impressions of textiles survived at Stěbořice; they may be remains of clothing. Remains of textiles caught on the outer sides of spurs are rather evidence of the wrapping of the dead in cloth, or the bottom of the grave may have been lined with textile (Jisl 1953). At Kráľovský Chlmec, during the analysis of charred remains of wood, fragments of leather were found, in two barrows, nos. 12 and 20. At this barrow cemetery animal bones were recorded in six mounds. In barrow no. 20 a small pit had been dug whose fill consisted only of calcined animal bones; in this case it is an offering in the form of an animal cremation grave (Budinský-Krička 1980). Only the barrow cemeteries in the Turiec region were richer – the barrows dug up in 1804 at Priekopa and in 1872 at Malý Čepčín. There V. Groó uncovered the barrow of a magnate buried in a coffin. His horse was reportedly buried together with him. Besides weapons (spears, arrows, an axe), a bridle consisting of a rod suspended in a ring, two stirrups and a prick spur also formed part of the grave. Of the whole find only three mounts have survived. Similar Carolingian spurs were present in the large barrows at Skalica as well (Eisner 1935).

blocks.alt: Barrow regions of the West Slavs in Central Europe and Slovakia

children.text: At Krásno nad Kysucou, at the locality known as Na kopcoch, two barrows were examined together with pupils of the local school; in one of the mounds a small stone idol was found which typologically recalls Early Slavic figures from the area of the Elbe Slavs.
The locations of the barrow cemeteries and their settlements.

The Slavs placed their barrow cemeteries on dominant elevations, on the tops of flat hills and the ridges of rises with a good view of the immediate surroundings, at an elevation of 400–600 m above sea level, and not in positions with a marked difference in height. In relation to the settlements, where any have been traced at all, the barrow cemeteries lie higher, on more prominent dominant features of the terrain. It seems that the settlements and their cemeteries, that is, the world of the living and the world of the dead, were separated by a natural obstacle, a boundary in the form of a valley, a stream or a river. In Slovakia above all, we hardly know any settlements with demonstrable links to the corresponding barrow cemetery. It is assumed that extensive barrow cemeteries such as Kráľovský Chlmec and Skalica served the inhabitants of several hamlets. The opposite situation occurs in the Prachov Rocks, where one hamlet used several barrow cemeteries. At the cemeteries of Slovakia the barrows are distributed irregularly; occasionally they form groups or are dispersed across the cemetery, and no application of any principle in their placing has been detected. An exception might be, for example, the kinship ties of those buried in a single group. The situation in Bohemia is different: at some cemeteries the barrows are arranged in regular rows, often running east–west. The locations of barrow cemeteries that no longer exist are attested only by surviving names such as Kopence at Bitarová, Homole at Nechvalín, Moholky at Súľov and Na Mohylky at Turany. Barrow cemeteries have survived at localities with the names Chlum, Chlmec, Na Kopcoch, Kopečnica, Kozárovské kopce, Háj, Panský háj, Hrobice, Homole and Homôlka.

children.text: The barrow cemeteries of Štefan Meliš

The barrow cemeteries of north-western Slovakia are concentrated around Sverepec, Beluša and Visolaje. Vojtech Budinský-Krička was the first to suggest the possibility of a boundary in this area between the North Slovak and the West Slovak tribe, when the excavations of the 1960s revealed the graves of warriors beneath the barrows at Visolaje and Sverepec. According to surviving tradition, the old main road also ran along this route, with the local names Súhradka (Svorádka), Markovec, Krčmiská and Rúsov laz, surrounded by the barrow cemeteries of Cesciny, Pravec, Panský háj and Podvrščie. Štefan Meliš found a larger solitary barrow in the village of Nosice at an elevation of 500 m above sea level; a cemetery with flat graves as well as burial beneath a barrow has therefore survived here. Between 1957 and 1962 most of the Slavic barrow cemeteries in the area were discovered by Štefan Meliš, an external collaborator of the Považie Museum, and examined by Anton Petrovský-Šichman. After the excavations were completed the barrows were heaped up again.

children.text:
Authors of the article: Stanislava Flimmelová, Orgoň.
 
 In the hradiska.sk editorial team we have at our disposal the locations of several barrows in north-western Slovakia which were found by Štefan Meliš and which, to the best of our knowledge, have not been published anywhere so far. We have, however, decided not to give their exact locations, in order to protect the barrows. Should archaeologists be interested, we will provide the data.
